title: Superconducting levitation and control of a high-reflectivity micromirror
authors: Philipp Koller, Jannek J. Hansen, David Walcher, Tomáš Plichta, Rémi Claessen, Martin Žemlička, Philip Schmidt, Rhys G. Povey, Stefan Minniberger, Stefan Putz, Markus Aspelmeyer, Michael Trupke
abstract: We introduce a method to suspend an optical micromirror, with a total mass of \SI{30}{\micro\gram}, using superconducting magnetic levitation. The micromirror is formed on a silicon membrane, coated with a high-reflectivity dielectric stack and attached to superconducting microspheres. The object is stably levitated inside a magnetic quadrupole field at cryogenic temperatures. Magnetic feedback on the transverse motion is used to stabilize the position of the levitator within the trapping field, allowing to measure the axial displacement of the levitator using optical interferometry. The system reaches a sensitivity of order \SI{100}{\pico\metre/\sqrt{\hertz}} near the axial trap frequency of \SI{167}{Hz}. This approach enables free-standing mirrors with minimal dissipation and tunable oscillation frequencies, offering a platform for precision sensing and quantum cavity optomechanics in the microgram regime.
summary: This paper presents a method to suspend and control a high-reflectivity micromirror using superconducting magnetic levitation at cryogenic temperatures. By employing active feedback and interferometric readout, the system achieves high sensitivity and stability, overcoming mechanical clamping losses. This establishes a versatile, low-dissipation platform crucial for advanced cavity optomechanics and quantum sensing.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the mechanical suspension of high-precision optical elements while minimizing environmental noise and dissipation.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated controlled superconducting magnetic levitation of a high-reflectivity micromirror, achieving high sensitivity and establishing a robust platform for cavity optomechanics.
method: The system uses superconducting anti-Helmholtz traps for levitation, combined with active feedback control (camera and intensity-based) to stabilize all three translational degrees of freedom.
model_or_system: The platform involves a microfabricated silicon mirror coated with a dielectric stack, levitated by superconducting microspheres within a magnetic quadrupole field at cryogenic temperatures. The motion is modeled by extending levitated sphere dynamics to a composite object.

main_assumptions: The measurements are limited by extrinsic heating (leading to quench) and the accuracy of the feedback control schemes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate fabrication steps, the experimental setup (cryostat, magnetic trap, interferometer), and the dependence of levitation time on trap current and optical probe power.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication process, the experimental setup for magnetic levitation, the implementation of multi-stage feedback control for motion stabilization, and the characterization of mechanical resonances and cavity performance.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges mechanical engineering, superconducting physics, and quantum optics, providing a highly controllable, low-loss mechanical element ideal for testing quantum ground states or coupling to quantum systems.
